course_title: Advanced Writing: Grammar, Syntax and Style

learning_outcomes.description: confidently identify grammatical features and patterns of contemporary written English
recognise grammatical choices that affect clarity, cohesion, and style
use your explicit knowledge of English grammar to reflect on and revise a variety of texts at both the structural and functional levels
integrate grammatical conventions to adapt, refine and polish writing for specific audiences, genres, and purposes.

Week 1 Wed - Week 13 Wed

Submit online via Blackboard
assessments.task_description:
The discussion component of this course evaluates how well you have understood the concepts covered in readings, lectures, and classes throughout the semester and how well you can recognise particular structures, written conventions, and potential errors. The task has been designed to encourage deep weekly engagement with course content and meaningful discussion among your peers.

You will participate in 10 online discussions across the semester. In each discussion thread, you will respond to a prompt and/or a classmate's contribution, receiving a mark between 1 and 3 depending on the accuracy and quality of your contribution. (Students who provide a substantial response – that is, demonstrate care and effort – should receive 3/3.)

Each discussion will open the same day as your lecture and remain open for 7 days, closing at 4.00 pm before the following week's lecture.

assessments.late_submission: A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
assessments.additional_info: You cannot defer or apply for an extension for this assessment.

assessments.assessment_title: Supervised tutorial problem set – structural and stylistic analysis
assessments.task_description:
This in-class assessment gives you an opportunity to apply your developing knowledge of English structure and style to a sample of published text.

On Monday morning ahead of the test date, you will gain access to a short passage of text, giving you an opportunity to annotate it and reflect on some of the ways the author has used words, phrases, and clauses (forms and structures) to achieve a particular style or effect. You may bring your annotated passage to the tutorial problem set, as well as one A4 page of notes and a print dictionary.

The tutorial problem set lasts for 90 minutes:

  • The first 10 minutes gives you perusal time, in which you can make initial notes about the three questions.
  • You will then have 20 minutes to discuss your observations and impressions with classmates.
  • The written component of this task then involves answering 3 questions about the text in paragraph form. You will have one hour (60 minutes) to write up your answers using the Inspera platform on your laptop.

assessments.task_description:
The final editing task gives you an opportunity to apply what you have learnt throughout the semester to an activity you might encounter in the workplace (or as a professional editor): marking up a passage of text with corrections and advice to the author.

This task is based loosely on the IPEd test for editors seeking accreditation in Australia. It's an excellent opportunity to gauge your current skill and accuracy as a writing and editing professional.

The task comprises 10 sequential blocks of text that contain a total of 30 errors or obvious weaknesses.

Your answer sheet will provide space for you to identify and describe each error or problem (for example, ‘spelling error—spell as X instead’ or ‘run-on sentence—insert semicolon’).

Each note is worth one mark for a total of 30/40 marks.

Your answer sheet will also provide space for you to re-write the entire passage to eliminate errors and improve clarity, tone, and structure, for a total of 10/40 marks.

To submit your assignment, you should upload your completed answer sheet and submit it via Turnitin. Please make sure your answers are as specific and coherent as possible. (Remember: imagine you are describing the problem to a client.)

To prepare for classes this week, read the resources published in the Week 2 folder.

Download a copy of the WRIT7260 glossary to add to throughout semester.

BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS

  • Why and how are words the building blocks of English sentences, and why does word order matter so much?

FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE

This lecture introduces you to the principles of audience awareness, genre sensitivity, and individual voice. It addresses the importance of word choice not only to convey meanings but also to craft a particular voice, persona, tone, style, and effect.

Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 2 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion.

learning_activities.topic:
Week 7: Understanding voice and using non-finite verb forms

In this tutorial, you'll consider the communicative options available to you when choosing between active and passive voice. You'll practise identifying non-finite verb forms in context and the ways they add extra action, dynamism, and dimension to our sentences. You'll also consider the ways authors use adverbs in their writing – and some additional conventions to be aware of as an editor, especially by avoiding misused modifiers.
